transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-12-18
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~75 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Owen Blake (Redwood SE), Priya Singh (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (AstroForge CTO), Marcus Hale (Head of ML), Dr. Samir Patel (Infra)
Meeting note: technical deep dive focused on long-context (128k+) runtime performance, chunking strategies, rotary/positional embedding behaviour, KV sharding, batching/latency tradeoffs, quantization options, and VPC/on-prem considerations.

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be incomplete):
- Discussed chunking vs append strategies for 128k+ prompts, memory & latency implications.
- Explored rotary embedding wrap/precision issues and mitigation (epochal slicing, positional rebase).
- KV cache sharding and persistent KV strategies to lower warm-start costs.
- Quantization tradeoffs (AWQ vs int8/int4) and kernel support on Redwood Dedicated.
- Plan: pilot run on Dedicated with sample dataset, share benchmark sheet and security docs.

Transcript Body:
00:00 Maya Chen: alright hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh quick roll call - sounds good on the audio?
00:06 Lena Ortiz: yep good here, thanks Maya
00:08 Marcus Hale: all good
00:10 Owen Blake: hey all, Owen from Redwood, I'll mostly cover the runtime bits today
00:14 Priya Singh: and Priya on the console/ops side
00:18 Maya Chen: great, today's agenda — we want to get into long-context ops, especially around your 128k+ prompts and how to keep steady latency while staying cost-effective. Lena, Marcus — can you reframe the primary goal?
00:30 Lena Ortiz: sure, we have multi-hour transcripts and telemetry that we want the model to attend to — like full session histories, 100–200k tokens in some cases. Success metric is sub-1.5s token step latency for interactive features and 95th percentile under 2s for generation across our main workstreams.
00:48 Marcus Hale: and cost target is ~30–40% reduction vs naive full-attend fp16 runs, otherwise we can't scale to prod
00:56 Owen Blake: understood. quick pointer: there are multiple levers—chunking plus smart KV caching, attention sparsity, and quantization. we'll try to map each to latency and quality tradeoffs.
01:08 Dr. Samir Patel: also note we need everything inside our VPC for now, on-prem readiness might be next quarter. encryption at rest via our KMS is a must.
01:18 Maya Chen: great, security constraints noted — we'll include the private deployment checklist.
01:25 Owen Blake: okay starting with chunking strategies — two high level patterns: sliding-append (append everything, rely on sparse attention and eviction) versus chunked-indexing (split into semantically coherent chunks and use retrieval to fetch relevant chunks into the prompt).
01:45 Marcus Hale: right, we tried append initially and ran into OOM and then token step latency blew up around 60k tokens, plus the rotary embeddings started to behave oddly.
02:00 Owen Blake: yes that matches our experience. append works to a point but at 128k+ you see rotary/rope wrap—like positional phase wrap—plus KV cache explosion. One mitigation is epochal slicing: we rebase positional encodings periodically and maintain multiple KV segments so the runtime only attends to a sliding window while still allowing long-recall via chunked retrieval.
02:28 Lena Ortiz: can you explain 'rebase' — do you mean rewriting positions on the fly? does that break attention coherence?
02:35 Owen Blake: good question — it's a careful transformation. we shift the base position of new tokens and keep a mapping layer for older segments. effectively the attention compute treats recent tokens with absolute positions and older segments as relative buckets. there's a small quality diff but we've tuned offsets to minimize hallucination. it's not magic but it keeps rotary from wrapping and avoids huge per-token compute.
03:05 Priya Singh: on Redwood, we implement this as multiple KV shards with a light metadata layer in the control plane. the runtime routes attention queries to the appropriate KV shard; we also have persistent KV options so you don't need to warm cache for every request.
03:20 Marcus Hale: persistent KV sounds promising — what's the storage backend? latency implications?
03:26 Owen Blake: persistent KV is stored in a memory-backed tier on Dedicated nodes with SSD-backed cold storage for eviction. For warm hits it's memory-local so we see sub-millisecond fetches. Cold fetches are tens to low hundreds of ms depending on SSD speed. In practice you can configure prewarm windows to avoid cold penalties for interactive flows.
03:48 Dr. Samir Patel: that sounds like a lot of ops state crossing into our VPC — is the control plane still hosted? we need private control plane for compliance.
03:56 Maya Chen: we support Private deployments — the control plane can be customer-managed in your VPC, and KMS integrations are supported. we'll share the on‑prem checklist.
04:06 Lena Ortiz: cool. back to chunking — for semantic chunking, what's the guidance for chunk size? we saw quality drop when we cut transcript into 2k token chunks.
04:18 Owen Blake: it's workload dependent. we recommend 4–8k token chunks for dense dialogue, larger for narrative text. More importantly, index overlapping boundaries (200–500 token overlap) and use a lightweight reranker to pick top-k chunks. That preserves context without full attention.
04:36 Marcus Hale: OK and attention sparsity — have you tested sparse/strided attention patterns vs full attention for 128k?
04:44 Owen Blake: yes. block-sparse and strided attention reduces compute but can harm coherence for some tasks. A hybrid approach works well: dense attention for the most recent 8–16k tokens, then strided/low-rank or global tokens for older segments. We've also prototyped learned-sparsity masks for certain LLMs, but that's more experimental and needs model recompile.
05:10 Priya Singh: quick note — we'll attach a couple of reference configs for the Redwood console showing how to set dense-window sizes and fallback policies.
05:18 Maya Chen: great — let's talk about rotary embedding edge cases because Marcus mentioned it.
05:22 Marcus Hale: yes, at ~70–80k tokens our generator began to produce repetitive positional artifacts, and perplexity increased subtly.
05:30 Owen Blake: that's classic RoPE phase roll-over. Two mitigations: (1) rebase positions as mentioned; (2) switch to ALiBi-style biases or hybrid position encodings. Each has tradeoffs — ALiBi can preserve monotonic distance but may change model calibration and needs evals. Rebase is lower risk on the serving side.
05:56 Lena Ortiz: does rebase imply modifying model weights?
06:00 Owen Blake: not usually — it's mostly a runtime positional transform. For some models small finetune helps but it's optional. We'll run the pilot both with runtime rebase and with a finetuned rebase variant so you can compare.
06:18 Maya Chen: ok next section — batching and latency. Marcus, you said interactive features need sub-1.5s token step. what's your concurrency pattern?
06:28 Marcus Hale: peak concurrency ~120 concurrent users during bursts, average ~30. Most interactions are short-live but some sessions keep generating for several minutes.
06:38 Owen Blake: batching aggressively reduces tokens/unit cost but increases tail latency. Redwood supports dynamic batching with latency budgets per route; for interactive flows we use small batch windows (8–12ms) and async prefixes. For analytic/background workflows you can use bigger batch windows to save cost.
06:56 Dr. Samir Patel: can we pin certain customers to dedicated queues to avoid noisy neighbors?
07:00 Priya Singh: yes that's a standard Dedicated mode feature — dedicated GPU pools with autoscale and burst options. You can set capacity constraints and routing rules at the token or route level.
07:12 Maya Chen: wanted to also touch quantization — Marcus mentioned AWQ, int8 and int4. What tradeoffs should we expect for 128k workloads?
07:22 Owen Blake: AWQ-int4 gives the most memory savings and enables larger effective context per GPU, but it's sensitive to rare-token distributions and can slightly degrade generation quality unless we use quant-aware kernels. int8/fp16 is safer quality-wise but more memory. On Redwood Dedicated we offer kernel selection for AWQ that pairs with specific attention kernels and KV layouts to avoid precision blowups. We'll include recommended model+quant combos in the benchmark sheet.
07:52 Marcus Hale: do we have perf numbers? like throughput and p95 latency for 128k with AWQ vs fp16?
08:00 Owen Blake: yes — high level: for a 128k sliding-window with dense recent 16k and chunked archive, AWQ-int4 reduced GPU memory by ~2.8x and lowered per-token compute cost by ~40% in our internal bench. P95 token-latency for interactive path (small batch windows) stayed around 1.2–1.8s depending on model size. We'll share more granular numbers in the spreadsheet.
08:26 Lena Ortiz: important to note our error budget — we need p95 under 2s for most routes otherwise feature gating kicks in.
08:34 Maya Chen: understood — the pilot will measure your p50/p95/p99 and cost per 1k tokens for each variant.
08:40 Owen Blake: another runtime trick: prefix KV caching for commonly requested prefixes reduces repeated attend cost. For your use case with repeated session starts, caching the first 8–16k tokens reduces cold start by 30–60%.
08:58 Marcus Hale: how do you handle eviction/persistence? we can't keep every session cached.
09:03 Owen Blake: eviction policies are LRU with TTLs and heuristics based on access frequency. For long-term recall we rely on chunked retrieval from persistent vector store and reconstruct a smaller prompt with the relevant chunks. If you want full global recall we also support tiered persistent KV where rarely accessed segments are on NVMe.
09:20 Dr. Samir Patel: what's the network egress pattern for persistent KV in private mode? we need to minimize cross-VPC egress.
09:28 Priya Singh: in Private deployments the KV and control plane components can be colocated inside your VPC, so egress is internal. For hosted/Routing variants we'd route through secure tunnels with encryption.
09:42 Maya Chen: question from our side — any special kernel flags you need or model ops that you already did on your side? Marcus:
09:48 Marcus Hale: we can compile models with flash-attention and have been testing custom CUDA kernels but we want to avoid heavy rebuilds if Redwood can handle kernel selection.
09:58 Owen Blake: Redwood runtime will select kernels based on model dims and SeqLen distribution; we can also accept your custom kernels but it's usually unnecessary. For AWQ and int4 we use optimized quantized GEMM and attention kernels; that keeps latency tight.
10:10 Lena Ortiz: you'd mentioned learned sparsity earlier; is that something we'd need to retrain for?
10:16 Owen Blake: typically yes, learned masks are trained or distilled, so it's more of an R&D path. For near-term the hybrid dense-window + strided older segments approach is lower risk.
10:30 Maya Chen: good. let's talk about observability — Marcus, what metrics do you need?
10:34 Marcus Hale: token-level latency distribution, KV cache hit rates, model version breakdown, cost per route, and per-session tracing for debugging. Also alerts for hallucination/regression for our key prompts.
10:46 Priya Singh: Redwood Console provides token-level charts, per-route dashboards, trace IDs, and an evals integration that runs prompt suites on deploys so you get regression alerts. We'll send a sample dashboard link after the call.
10:58 Lena Ortiz: perfect. compliance — Dr. Patel again — we need SOC2 documentation, detailed audit logs, and KMS integration notes.
11:08 Maya Chen: we'll attach SOC2, the on-prem checklist, and the KMS integration guide. In Private deployments the logs can remain in your audit storage.
11:16 Dr. Samir Patel: and data residency? we need EU region only for some datasets.
11:20 Priya Singh: you can pin region and route rules; Dedicated clusters can be provisioned in a region you specify. For Private you control the cluster location entirely.
11:28 Marcus Hale: couple more quick items — what about fallback strategies if a model variant hits OOM mid-batch?
11:34 Owen Blake: our runtime supports graceful fallback to a smaller model variant, or to a lower precision kernel. We also do per-request slice checks and can abort and retry with a different routing policy. That is configurable per-route in the console.
11:48 Lena Ortiz: sounds sensible. Also want to know about A/B and canary for these long-context changes — we don't want to risk production regressions.
11:56 Maya Chen: Redwood supports canary rollouts and traffic splitting by percentage and by user segment; you'd run the AWQ variant on 5% of traffic first, compare logs and eval metrics, then ramp.
12:06 Marcus Hale: ok let's confirm pilot plan then.
12:10 Maya Chen: proposed pilot — Redwood will run three variants on a Dedicated test pool: fp16 baseline (append+dense), AWQ-int4 with epochal slicing + persistent KV, and hybrid chunked-indexing with retrieval. We'll run your 3 datasets for 48 hours and collect p50/p95/p99, cost per 1k tokens, KV hit rates, and a handful of generated outputs for manual eval.
12:32 Lena Ortiz: timeline?
12:34 Owen Blake: we can have the Dedicated test queue up in 48 hours pending contract, but for this pilot we can use a short-term test credit cluster and get started within 24–48 hours. We'll need your datasets and SLOs.
12:44 Maya Chen: action items recap — Maya to send benchmarks and doc links, Owen to provision test pool and run initial model comparators, Lena to share datasets and SLOs.
12:56 Marcus Hale: thanks — one more question: for the rotary rebase approach do you have a guide for when to rebase (token thresholds) and how to tune overlap?
13:06 Owen Blake: yes — typical heuristics are rebase every 16–32k tokens with 1–2k overlap; we tune based on evaluation on your prompt set. We'll include recommended defaults in the runbook.
13:18 Lena Ortiz: thank you — that helps a lot.
13:22 Maya Chen: perfect, we'll follow up with the spreadsheet and schedule the pilot start. thanks everyone.
